issues.legal_issue: The statutory ceiling on land held for personal cultivation applies whenever a landowner or tenant holds land above the permissible limit, including when the excess arises after the ceiling provisions take effect.
material_facts: Land that had been mortgaged with possession was excluded from the landowner’s holding for the ceiling calculation while the mortgage subsisted.
After the landowner redeemed the mortgage and regained possession, his total holding exceeded the permissible limit.
The revenue authorities sought surrender of the excess land, although the Act then provided no express machinery for this type of case.
issues.conclusion: The landowner became liable to surrender the surplus land under the ceiling provision; the absence of an express procedure did not permit the court to disregard the provision’s plain terms.
issues.legal_principle: Section 32-A imposes a continuing ceiling on land held for personal cultivation, not merely a ceiling measured when the provision came into force. The Court followed Vidya Vati v. The State of Punjab & Ors., which held that the ban applies whenever a person is found to hold land in personal cultivation above the permissible limit. Sections 32-L and 32-M address particular kinds of later acquisitions but do not restrict section 32-A’s general operation. A court must give effect to section 32-A’s plain words even where express enforcement machinery is absent.

predicates.land_ceiling_proceeding: The matter concerns whether land held above a permissible ceiling must be surrendered.
predicates.personal_holding_exceeds_permissible_lim: A landowner or tenant holds land for personal cultivation in excess of the applicable permissible limit.

issues.definition: When a land-ceiling proceeding concerns a personal holding above the permissible limit, the excess land must be surrendered.

issues.legal_issue: Redemption of a mortgage with possession is not a transfer within the meaning of the restriction on future transfers.
material_facts: The landowner had mortgaged land with possession but retained ownership and the equity of redemption.
On redeeming the mortgage, the landowner regained possession of the land.
The High Court treated the regained possession as an acquisition by transfer under the restriction on future acquisitions.
issues.conclusion: Redemption did not amount to a transfer within the meaning of section 32-L, although the land regained on redemption counted toward the landowner’s holding under section 32-A.
issues.legal_principle: In the context of section 32-L, “transfer” does not include the return of possession to a mortgagor on redemption. The mortgagor does not cease to be the owner when land is mortgaged with possession; the equity of redemption remains with the mortgagor. The Court applied sections 32-A and 32-L and relied on Vidya Vati v. The State of Punjab & Ors. for the broader principle that the general ceiling provision continues to operate despite provisions addressing particular later acquisitions.

predicates.land_ceiling_proceeding: The matter concerns the application of a land ceiling to a holding affected by a later change in possession.
predicates.possession_mortgage_redeemed: A mortgagor redeems a mortgage under which the mortgagee held possession and regains possession of the land.
predicates.mortgagor_retained_ownership: The mortgagor remained the owner of the land and retained the right to redeem it while the mortgage subsisted.

issues.definition: In a land-ceiling proceeding, when a mortgagor who retained ownership redeems a possession mortgage and regains possession, that redemption is not a prohibited transfer.
